SCENES OF ACTION

row.cell: AT THE BOTTOM OF THE RHINE
OPEN SPACE ON A MOUNTAIN HEIGHT NEAR THE RHINE
OPEN SPACE AS IN SCENE II.

div.head: At the bottom of the Rhine

p.hi: A greenish twilight, lighter above than below. The upper part is filled with undulating water, which streams respectively from right to left. Towards the bottom the waves resolve themselves into a mist which grows finer as it descends, so that a space, as high as a mans body from the ground, appears to be quite free from the water, which floats like a train of clouds over the gloomy stretch below. Steep rocky peaks jut up everywhere from the depths, and enclose the entire stage. The ground is a wild confusion of jagged rocks, no part of it being quite level, and on every side deeper fisures are indicated by a still denser gloom. Woglinde circles with graceful swimming movements round the central rock.

lg.l: If Wellgunde came we were two.

div.p: [They playfully tease and chase one another.

lg.l: Help me to hinder her flying.
FLOSSHILDE [Dives down between the two at play.
Or dear you'll pay for your sport!

div.p: [They swim asunder with merry cries. Flosshilde tries to catch first the one, then the other. They elude her, and then combine to chase her, darting like fish from rock to rock with jests and laughter. Meanwhile Alberich climbs out of a dark ravine on to a rock. He pauses, still surrounded by darkness, and watches the frolic of the Rhine-Maidens with increasing pleasure.

lg.l: Would ye be kind to me.

div.p: [The maidens, as soon as they hear Alberich's voice, stop playing.
[They dive down and see the Nibelung.
The frolic of the Rhine-Maidens.
[Both the others follow her, and all three gather quickly round the central rock.

lg.l: Would join in your frolic and play.
Glide down, how close in my arms

div.p: [She sinks down to the top of the rock, whose base Alberich has reached.
[Climbs with gnome-like agility, though with repeated checks, to the summit of the rock. Irritably.
[He has got near Woglinde.
[He tries to embrace her.
[She swims up to another rock.

lg.l: WOGLINDE [Swims to a third rock lower down.
WOGLINDE [Darts upwards to a higher rock at the side.
Ha! ha! ha! ha! ha! ha!

div.p: [He tries to climb after her in haste.
WELLGUNDE
[Has sunk down to a lower rock on the other side.
[Climbs hastily over the river-bottom towards Wellgunde.
[Sinking down till she is a little nearer him.

lg.l: To thy bosom with love and with longing.

div.p: [Tries to detain her by force
[Swimming up quickly to the middle rock.

lg.l: Hold firm, or I will escape!
Ha! ha! ha! ha! ha! ha!
Hei! if I am so loathsome
Give thy love to the eels!
Fain at a word to grant!
The chance is I charm one of many,
Whilst, single, no one would choose me!
Not to see he is fair!

div.p: [She draws him tenderly towards her.

lg.l: To be pierced by thy glance,
To be pricked by thy beard,
To see and to feel them for aye!
Might thy hair hard as bristles
And thy form like a frog's,
And the croak of thy voice—
O could I, dumb with amaze,

div.p: [Dive down close to them and laugh.

lg.l: Ha! ha! ha! ha! ha! ha!

div.p: A suitable end to the song.
[She swims up quickly with her sisters.

lg.l: Ha! ha! ha! ha! ha! ha!
Alone, O ye false nixie brood?
Cease, and do as we bid thee!
The maid, when won, more fast?
In the waves we scarce can escape.

div.p: [They swim apart hither and thither, now lower, now higher, to provoke Alberich to give chase.
The Rhine-Maidens teasing Alberich.

lg.l: So laugh and lie your fill—
And one must yield to my yearning!

div.p: [He starts chasing them with desperate energy. He climbs with terrible agility, and, springing from rock to rock, tries to catch one maiden after another. They keep eluding him with mocking laughter. He stumbles and falls into the abyss, and clambers up quickly again and resumes the chase. They sink down a little towards him; he almost reaches them, but falls, back again, and once more tries to catch them. At last he pauses out of breath, and, foaming with rage, stretches his clenched fist up towards the maidens.

lg.l: If but this fist had one!

div.p: [He remains speechless with rage, gazing upwards, when he is suddenly attracted and arrested by the following spectacle. Through the water a light of continually increasing brilliance breaks from above, and, at a point near the top of the middle rock, kindles to a radiant and dazzling golden gleam. A magical light streams from this through the waves.

lg.l: The wakener laughs to the deep.

div.p: [Swimming gracefully round the cliff together.

lg.l: Wallala la la la leia jahei!
How glorious and glad thy smile,
We dive and encircle thy bed!
Wallala la la la heia jahei!

div.p: [With increasing mirthful abandonment the maidens swim round the rock. The water is filled with a glimmering golden light.
ALBERICH
[Whose eyes, strongly attracted by the radiance, stare fixedly at the gold.

lg.l: Where dost thou hail from, O churl,
Of the Rhinegold not to have heard?
That wakes and sleeps in turn?
Come, float and frolic with us!
Did he but know all its wonders!
That no thief from the water might steal it.
Can hope to fashion the gold?
Can learn and master the magic
That makes a ring of the gold.
For love is part of living;
No one would live without loving.

div.p:
"Mock away! Mock away!
The Niblung makes for your toy!"

lg.l: O come, lovely one, laugh as we laugh!
Wallala la la la leia jahei!

div.p: [They swim, laughing, backwards and forwards in the light.
ALBERICH
[His eyes fixed on the gold, has listened attentively to the sisters rapid chatter.

lg.l: The whole earth inherit through thee?

div.p: [In a terribly loud voice.

lg.l: The Niblung makes for your toy!

div.p: [Raging he springs on to the middle rock, and clambers to the top. The maidens scatter, screaming, and swim upwards on different sides.

lg.l: Ha! ha! ha! ha! ha! ha! ha!

div.p: [Reaching the top with a last spring.
[He stretches his hand out towards the gold.

lg.l: I tear the gold from the rock;
Forged be the ring for revenge!
I forswear love and curse it!

div.p: [He tears the gold from the rock with terrific force, and immediately plunges with it into the depths, where he quickly disappears. Sudden darkness envelops the scene. The maidens dive down after the robber.

[The water sinks with them. From the lowest depth Alberich's shrill, mocking laughter rings up. The rocks are hidden by impenetrable darkness. The whole stage from top to bottom is filled with black waves, which for some time appear to sink even lower.

div.head: SECOND SCENE

p.hi: The waves have gradually changed into clouds which, becoming lighter and lighter by degrees, finally disperse in a fine mist. As the mist vanishes upwards in light little clouds an open space on a mountain height becomes visible in the dim light which precedes dawn. At one side Wotan with Fricka beside him both asleep, lie on a flowery bank. The dawning day illumines with increasing brightness a castle with glittering pinnacles which stands on the summit of a cliff in the background. Between this and the foreground a deep valley is visible through which the Rhine flows.

div.p: FRICKA
[Awakes; her gaze falls on the castle, which has become plainly visible; alarmed.

lg.l: Is guarded by gate and door:

div.p: [Awakes and raises himself slightly. His glance is immediately arrested by the view of the castle.

lg.l: As I nursed it in dream
The price that was to be paid?
Hast thou then no care for the cost?
With them who built the abode.
Fret not thou, counting the cost.
Had I but known of thy pact,
The trick had never been played;
That, deaf to us and in peace,
Alone ye might deal with the giants.
Herself when the castle she craved?
I was forced to ponder some means
True to me when his fancy
Tempted him far from his home.
But thou hadst the work designed
To stir up to tumult still fiercer
That built were the towering walls
To me, the god, must be granted,
And conquer the world from without.
That sport at least thou must leave me.
When I went wooing, to win thee
What folly now then to scold!

div.p: [ Anxiously looking towards a point not on the stage.
[Enters as if flying from someone.

lg.l: He comes to bear me off captive.
Though from his snares thou hast suffered.
Can teach, as by Loge employed.
On him my faith I have fixed.
And art left in the lurch.
When help ye should bring me,
Weak and bartered away by my kin?
Now the knaves who plotted and tricked thee

div.p: [Fasolt and Fafner, both of gigantic stature, enter, armed with stout clubs.
[Pointing to the castle.

p.hi: Stands for a space speechless with angry surprise.

lg.l: All the runes of solemn bargain?
Fool, dost now see the trick?
There are bounds to thy might.
Stand fast by a bargain once fixed.
O wise one, take it from him!

div.p: Freia, the fair one

lg.l: How sly to judge us serious
When plainly we were but jesting!
For churls what charm could she have?
Price of walls and of halls!
And ye call the pact a jest?
No gain look we to get.
If from the Gods we remove her.
Grows the apples and tends them.

div.p: [Roughly.

lg.l: From their midst, therefore, Freia must forth!

div.p: [Fafner and Fasolt press towards Freia. Froh and Donner enter in haste.

lg.l: Help! Help from the harsh ones!

div.p: [To Fafner.

lg.l: With what weight my hammer falls?
We want but our due reward.

div.p: [He swings his hammer.
WOTAN
[Stretching out his spear between the combatants.
[Turns away and sees Loge coming.
[Has come up out of the valley in the background.

lg.l: They dream but of roof and room:
A home in which to dwell,
Who calls me sluggard, he lies!
In the gang that trusted thee not.
Now speak, and to the point!
For when the builders at first

div.p: [Donner threatens to strike Loge.
WOTAN
[Stepping between them.

lg.l: Both in weight and in worth.

div.p: [Turns sternly to Loge.

lg.l: How far hast thou ranged and roamed?
To the ends of the earth
To find a ransom for Freia
Fair to the giants and just.
That a man will take it instead

div.p: [All seem surprised and taken aback.

lg.l: Where life moves and has being,
But where life moves and has being

div.p: [Varied gestures of amazement.

lg.l: That thy wrath may fall on the robber
They would have thee grant them
To guard in the water for ever.
And, keeping faith, he has told.
What help have I for others?

div.p: [Who has been listening attentively, to Fafner.

lg.l: The Niblung has much annoyed us;
I greatly grudge him this Rhinegold;
But such his craft and cunning,
What wondrous gift has the gold,
That the dwarf desires it so?
It wins its owner the world.
Be worn by a woman too?
That charm which dwarfs are welding,
Working in thrall to the ring.

div.p: [As if falling more and more under the influence of a spell.

lg.l: Won I the ring to my service.
To forge and fashion it true?
Yet plain the spell to him

div.p: [Wotan turns away in annoyance.
[Harshly.

lg.l: And wrought aright was the ring.
Were not the ring from him wrested.
Without cursing love it were won.
Without guile, as in children's games!
How better could object be won?
If the thief thou wouldst confound,

div.p: [With warmth.

lg.l: For this they pray and implore.
Full many a man to their caves.

div.p: [Wotan stands silent, struggling with himself. The other Gods gaze at him in mute suspense. Fafner, meanwhile, has been consulting aside with Fasolt.

lg.l: Who could use the charm in its quest.

div.p: [Fasolt's gestures indicate that he is being convinced against his will. Fafner and Fasolt approach Wotan again.

lg.l: How can I, shameless ones, pay you?
The Niblung to break and bind!

div.p: Fasolt suddenly seizes Freia and drags her to one side with Fafner

lg.l: Dolts you grow through my debt!

div.p: [Suddenly seizes Freia and drags her to one side with Fafner.

lg.l: As pledge thou shalt be held
As a pledge she is ours.
If the Rhinegold be not ready,
And bides among us for aye!

div.p: [The giants hasten off, dragging Freia with them.
[They look inquiringly at Wotan.

lg.l: Through the ford across the Rhine
The louts, how they lumber along!
Through the Rhine valley they reel.

div.p: [He turns to the Gods.

lg.l: What ails the high, happy Gods?

div.p: [A pale mist, gradually increasing in density, fills the stage. Seen through it the Gods look more and more wan and aged. All stand in dismay and apprehension regarding Wotan, whose eyes are fixed broodingly on the ground.

lg.l: Lo! the bloom forsakes your cheeks,
And quenched is the light of your eyes!
Has made him gloomy and old?

div.p: The Gods grow wan and aged at the loss of Freia.

lg.l: I have it: hear what ye lack!
Restored you your strength and your youth,
Am I, ye high ones, as you!

div.p: [Freely, but quickly and harshly.

lg.l: To the fruit that makes young,
As well both the giants wist.
Wasting, the scoff of the world,
The Gods must pine and pass.
WOTAN [Coming to a sudden resolve, starts up.
I go in search of the gold.
Not vainly they hoped for thy help then?
Sheer through the depths of the Rhine?

div.p: [He goes in front and vanishes at the side through a cleft, from which, immediately afterwards, sulphurous vapour streams forth.

lg.l: When got will again make us young.

div.p: [He descends after Loge into the chasm. The sulphurous vapour which rises from it spreads over the whole stage and quickly fills it with thick clouds. Those who remain behind are soon hidden.

[The sulphurous vapour darkens till it becomes a black cloud, which rises upwards from below. This then changes to a dark, rocky cavern which keeps rising, so that the stage seems to sink deeper and deeper into the earth.

div.head: THIRD SCENE

p.hi: From various points in the distance ruddy lights gleam out. An increasing clamour, as of smiths at work, is heard on all sides. The clang of the anvils dies away. A vast subterranean chasm becomes visible which seems to open into narrow gorges on all sides. Alberich drags the screaming Mime out of a side cleft.

lg.l: Take but thy nails from my ear!

div.p: [He tries to catch hold of his ear again. In his terror Mime drops a piece of metal-work which he has been clutching convulsively. Alberich picks it up hastily and examines it with care.
[He puts the Tarnhelm on his head.

lg.l: But will the spell prosper too?

div.p: [Very softly.
[He vanishes, and a pillar of cloud takes his place.

lg.l: Where art thou? I see no one.
Take that for thy thievish thoughts!

div.p: [Writhes under the lathes he receives, the sound of which is heard without the whip being seen.

lg.l: Thy work has stood the test.
None shall escape from his thraldom!

div.p: [Harshly.
[The pillar of cloud disappears in the background. Alberich's scolding voice is heard more and more faintly. Mime lies huddled up in pain. Wotan and Loge come down through a cleft in the rock.

lg.l: How bright yonder fiery sparks glimmer!

div.p: Mime writhes under the lashes he receives.

lg.l: Who beats and bullies thee so?

div.p: [He raises him with difficulty.

lg.l: For I am bound as his slave.
This spell puts in his power
And lightly laughed at our toil.
To heap up higher his hoard.
The master himself I had mastered,
And, he in my power, had wrested
The ring from him and used it
That he might serve me, the free man,

div.p: [Harshly

lg.l: As now I must serve him, a slave!
Ah! though the helm I fashioned,

div.p: [Howling and sobbing.
[He rubs his back. Wotan and Loge laugh.

lg.l: Will free all the Nibelung folk.
MIME [Shrinking back in fear when he hears Alberich returning.

div.p: [He runs to and fro in terror.

[He sits down calmly on a stone. Alberich, who has taken the Tarnhelm from his head and hung it on his girdle, is brandishing his scourge and driving before him a band of Nibelungs from the gorges below. These are laden with gold and silver treasure, which, urged on by Alberich, they pile up so as to form a large heap.
[He suddenly perceives Wotan and Loge.

lg.l: Back to thy bellows and beating!

div.p: [Lashing Mime, he chases him into the crowd of Nibelungs.

lg.l: Of my whip will find him;
That where no one would guess
None knows it better than he.

div.p: Alberich drives in a band of Nibelungs laden with gold and silver treasure.
[He pulls the ring from his finger, kisses it and stretches it out in menace.
[Howling and shrieking, the Nibelungs, among them Mime, scatter, and creep down into the clefts in all directions.
ALBERICH
[Looks long and distrustfully at Wotan and Loge.

lg.l: Had Loge not smiled on thee?
Had not I heated thy forge?
Art thou, false one, their friend
As my friend thou wert once,
No harm from such need I fear.
No cause then for thy distrust.

div.p: [Taking up a defiant attitude.

lg.l: Yet I dare you all unflinching.
A richer one never was seen.
But what is gained by the hoard
Where wealth finds nothing to buy?
And win the whole world and its fairness.
But, my friend, how compass that goal?
Ye who live above and breathe
Ere long, O ye Gods, will have gripped you!
As I forswore love, even so
For gold alone will his greed be.
The dwarf will force to his will,

div.p: [Laughing savagely.

lg.l: Beware of the hosts of the night,
When rise shall the Nibelung hoard
From silent depths to the day!

div.p: [To Alberich.

lg.l: Who would gaze not in wonder,
If only thy skill can achieve
Almighty I needs must acclaim thee!
And the sun in his glory,
But what would seem of most moment
Is that they who serve thee,
When thy hand held forth a ring
Thy folk were stricken with fear.
Say, how wouldst thou save thyself then?
Most shrewd to himself seems Loge;
If I had to ask for
How happy the thief would be!
Even from thee I am safe,
Decide to what I shall change;
In that form I shall stand.
But strike me dumb with amaze.
ALBERICH [Puts the Tarnhelm on his head.

div.p: [He immediately disappears. An enormous serpent writhes on the floor in his place. It rears and threatens Wotan and Loge with its open jaws.

lg.l: Ha! ha! ha! ha! ha! ha!
Spare the life of poor Loge!
The dwarf to the dragon immense!

div.p: [The dragon disappears and, in its stead, Alberich is again seen in his own shape.

lg.l: Spare the life of poor Loge!"
My trembling tells thee how truly.
That, though, I fear were too hard!
The most cramped of crannies must hold thee

div.p: [He puts the Tarnhelm on his head again.
[He vanishes. The Gods see a toad on the rocks creeping towards them.
[Wotan sets his foot on the toad. Loge makes a dash at its head and holds the Tarnhelm in his hand.
ALBERICH
[Is suddenly seen in his own shape writhing under Wotan's foot.
[Loge binds his hands and feet with a rope.
[Both seize hold of the prisoner, who struggles violently, and drag him towards the shaft by which they descended. They disappear mounting upwards.

div.head: FOURTH SCENE

p.hi: The scene has changed as before, only in reverse order. Open space on mountain heights. The prospect is veiled by pale mist as at the end of the second scene. Wotan and Loge climb up out of the cavern, bringing with them Alberich bound.

lg.l: That was thine for the winning, thou fool!
Wilt give to me for my stall?

div.p: [He dances round Alberich, snapping his fingers.

lg.l: Or dear for this outrage shalt answer!
And all that the world containeth,
Thou liest bound at my feet,
And, coward, canst not deny it.

div.p: [He shows him the kind of ransom by snapping his fingers.

lg.l: The hoard and thy gleaming gold.

div.p: [Aside.

lg.l: If I only can keep the ring,
The hoard I can lightly let go,
For anew I could win it
By the powerful spell of the ring.
The warning will not have been lost,
Even though lost may be the gold.

div.p: [Loge frees his right hand.
ALBERICH
[Touches the ring with his lips and secretly murmurs the command.

lg.l: With the hoard from the depths to the day.
Nay, first in full thou must pay.

div.p: [The Nibelungs come up out of the cleft laden with the objects of which the hoard is composed.

lg.l: Should see me captive and bound!

div.p: [To the Nibelungs.

lg.l: For I follow hard at your heels!

div.p: [He kisses the ring and holds it out with an air of command. As struck with a blow, the Nibelungs press terrified and cowering towards the cleft, down which they hastily disappear.

lg.l: That also pray give me again!

div.p: [Throwing the Tarnhelm on to the heap.

lg.l: The plunder must pay for the pardon.
My cunning defence to the foe!
That also belongs to the hoard.
My life—but the ring: not that!
For thy life I care not at all.
But if my life I ransom
The ring I must also rescue
Than mine is the ruddy ring!
The ring thou claimest as thine?
Was as gift to thee given
That thou didst thieve for the ring!
The sin so sweet to thyself?
Bereft the Rhine of its gold,
As easy to forge as to steal!
Was fired into winning the spell
My ban bringing blessing to thee?

div.p: [He seizes Alberich and draws the ring from his finger by force.

lg.l: I own what makes me supreme,
The mightiest lord of all lords!

div.p: [He puts on the ring.

lg.l: Greeting take, for it is thine!
As a curse gave me the ring,
My curse go with the ring!
Be he who shall hold it,
Those who guard it nothing shall gain,
Yet shall murder go where they go.
By fetters of fear shall be bound;
In my hand the gold I was robbed of.

div.p: [Laughing.
Keep it with care;
[Grimly.
From my curse none shall escape!
[He vanishes quickly through the cleft. The thick mist in the foreground gradually clears away.

lg.l: WOTAN [Left in contemplation of the ring.
Grudge him not vent to his spleen!

div.p: [It keeps growing lighter.
[Through the vanishing mist Donner, Froh, and Fricka appear, and hasten towards the foreground.

lg.l: Sad, forlorn had our lot been,

div.p: [Fasolt and Fafner enter, leading Freia between them. Fricka hastens joyfully towards her sister. The foreground has become quite bright again, the light restoring to the aspect of the Gods its original freshnesh. The background, however, is still veiled by the mist so that the distant castle remains invisible.

lg.l: Once more for mine have I won thee!
And that my heart may forget her
The blossom-sweet maid from mine eyes!

div.p: [Freia is placed in the middle by the two giants, who then stick their staves into the ground in front of her so that her height and breadth is indicated.

lg.l: Thus high now heap ye the hoard.

div.p: [Loge and Froh heap up the treasure hastily between the staves.
[He presses down the treasure with rude strength; he bends down to look for gaps.

lg.l: Come here! This gap must be closed!
The lovely one owes this to thee!
Still more! Pile on still more.
Thy strength then measure with mine!
It will crush thee to thy cost, rogue.

div.p: [Measures the hoard carefully with his eye, and looks to see if there are any crevices.

lg.l: Still shines to me Holda's hair.
LOGE [Throws the Tarnhelm on the heap.

div.p: [He goes up to the hoard and peers through it.
[Beside himself.

lg.l: While her sweet eyes I behold thus,
From the woman how can I part?
Give that to close up the crevice!
Wotan will give them what theirs is.
The ring I won so hardly,
Undismayed I hold and will keep.
I gave the maidens who grieved.
By thy promise I am not bound;
As booty mine is the ring.
The world would I give you the ring.
FASOLT [Furious, pulls Freia from behind the hoard.
Fair Freia ours is for ever!

div.p: [Fafner stops Fasolt as he is hastening off. All stand dismayed; Wotan turns from them in anger. The stage has grown dark again. From a cleft in the rock on one side issues a bluish flame in which Erda suddenly becomes visible, rising so that her upper half is seen.

lg.l: ERDA [Stretching out a warning hand towards Wotan.
All things that were I know,
Nightly the Norns tell to Wotan.
Be counselled; keep not the ring!

div.p: [Erda sinks slowly as far as the breast, while the bluish light grows fainter.
[She vanishes completely.
"Erda bids thee beware"
[Wotan is about to follow Erda in order to detain her. Froh and Fricka throw themselves in his way and prevent him.
[Wotan gazes thoughtfully before him.

lg.l: DONNER [Turning to the giants with a resolute air.
The gold we give you also.

div.p: [All look at Wotan in suspense; he, rousing himself from deep thought, grasps his spear and swings it in token of having come to a bold decision.

lg.l: Here, giants, take ye the ring!

div.p: [He throws the ring on the hoard. The giants release Freia; she hastens joyfully to the Gods, who caress her in turns for a space, with every manifestation of delight.

lg.l: More on the maid than the gold
Thou wouldst have wooed for thy bride;
That the most of it should be mine.

div.p: [To the Gods.
[Wotan turns away in contempt.

lg.l: Hold to what matters: the ring!

div.p: [Falls upon Fafner, who has meanwhile been steadily packing up the treasure.

lg.l: I lost for it Freia's smile.

div.p: [He snatches haply at the ring.
[There is a struggle. Fasolt tears the ring from Fafner.

lg.l: I hold it. It is mine now!
Hold fast, lest it should fall!

div.p: [Lunging out with his stave, he fells Fasolt to the ground with one blow; from the dying man he then hastily tears the ring.

lg.l: No more shalt thou touch the ring!

div.p: [He puts the ring into the sack and tranquilly continues to pack up the rest of the hoard. All the Gods stand horrified. A solemn silence.
Fafner kills Fasolt.

lg.l: I find is the curse's might.
But the gain of its loss
For the gold thou hast let go.
DONNER [Pointing to the background, which is still
Charged with their storms I will gather,
And sweep the blue heavens clean.

div.p: [Donner mounts a high rock on the edge of the precipice, and swings his hammer; during what follows the mists gather round him.

lg.l: Hey da! Hey da! Hey do!

div.p: [He swings his hammer.

lg.l: Donner, your lord, summons his hosts!
Hey da! Hey da! Hey do!

div.p: [Donner disappears completely in a thunder-cloud which has been growing darker and denser. The stroke of his hammer is heard falling heavily on the rock. A vivid flash of lightning comes from the cloud, followed by a loud clap of thunder. Froh has also disappeared in the cloud.

lg.l: Show them the way by the bridge!

div.p: [Suddenly the clouds roll away. Donner and Froh become visible. A rainbow of dazzling radiance stretches from their feet across the valley to the castle, which is gleaming in the light of the setting sun.
FROH
[Who, with outstretched hand, indicates to the Gods that the bridge is the way across the valley.

lg.l: Leads the bridge to your halls.

div.p: [Wotan and the other Gods stand speechless, lost in contemplation of the glorious sight.

lg.l: Donner, your lord, summons his hosts!"
And fear have gone to the winning!

div.p: [Very firmly, as if struck by a great thought.
[He turns solemnly to Fricka.

lg.l: I never seem to have heard it.

div.p: [He takes Fricka's hand and walks slowly with her towards the bridge. Froh, Freia, and Donner follow.

lg.l: LOGE [Remaining in the foreground and looking
They are hasting on to their end,
They who dream they are strong and
Yes, even if godlike the Gods were—

div.p: [With a show of carelessness he goes to the Gods.

lg.l: THE THREE RHINE-MAIDENS [From the valley. Invisible.
Once thou didst shine on us!
O give us the Rhinegold again!
WOTAN [About to set his foot on the bridge, pauses and turns round.
What wailing sound do I hear?
Bid them tease us no more!
In the Gods' increase of splendour

div.p: [The Gods laugh and cross the bridge during what follows.

lg.l: There but shone still our treasure pure!

div.p: [As the Gods cross the bridge to the castle the curtain falls.

div.head: THE VALKYRIE
div.p: CHARACTERS
SCENES OF ACTION

lg.l: ACT I. THE INTERIOR OF HUNDING'S DWELLING
ACT II. A WILD ROCKY MOUNTAIN
ACT III. ON THE TOP OF A ROCKY MOUNTAIN

div.head: THE FIRST ACT

p.hi: The interior of a dwelling-place built of wood, with the stem of a mighty ash-tree as its centre; to the right, in the foreground, is the hearth, and behind this the store-room. At the back is the large entrance door; to the left, far back, steps lead up to an inner chamber; on the same side, nearer the front, stands a table with a broad bench behind it, fixed to the wall, and with stools in front. The stage remains empty for a space. Outside a storm is just subsiding. Siegmund opens the entrance door from without, and enters. With his hand on the latch he surveys the room. He seems overwhelmed with fatigue; his dress and appearance indicate that he is in flight. He shuts the door behind him when he sees nobody, walks to the hearth with the final effort of an utterly exhausted man, and throws himself down on a bearskin rug.

div.p: [He sinks back and remains stretched out motionless. Sieglinde enters from the inner chamber; she thinks her husband has returned. Her grave look changes to one of surprise when she sees the stranger stretched out on the hearth.
[Coming nearer.
[As Siegmund does not move, she draws nearer still and looks at him.
[She bends over him, and listens.
[She takes a drinking-horn and hurries out. She returns with it full, and offers it to Siegmund.
[Siegmund drinks, and hands her back the horn. As he signifies his thanks with a movement of the head, he gazes at her with growing interest.

lg.l: Who soothes and comforts me so?
Stay thou here as his guest;
Quick, show me! Where are thy wounds?

div.p: [Shakes himself and springs up briskly to a sitting posture.

lg.l: My limbs are well knit still,
If my spear and shield had but been
Half so strong as my arm is,
But in splinters were spear and shield.
But, faster than I from foemen,
Darkness fell deep on my lids,
But now the sun again laughs.

div.p: [Goes to the storeroom, fills a horn with mead, and proffers it to Siegmund with friendly eagerness.

lg.l: Set it first to thy lips.

div.p: [Sieglinde sips from the horn and hands it back to him. Siegmund takes a long draught, regarding Sieglinde with increasing warmth. Still gazing, he takes the horn from his lips and lets it sink slowly, while his features express strong emotion. He sighs deeply, and lowers his gaze gloomily to the ground.

lg.l: Thou hast tended an ill-fated one!

div.p: [He starts up quickly, and goes towards the the back.

lg.l: Who pursues thee so close at thy heels?
Be thou preserved from its touch!
I must not gaze but go.

div.p: [He strides hastily to the door and lifts the latch.

lg.l: SIEGLINDE [Forgetting herself calls impetuously after him.
To those who abide with it!

div.p: SIEGMUND

[Deeply moved, remains standing; he looks searchingly at Sieglinde, who, ashamed and sad, lowers her eyes. Returning, he leans against the hearth, his gaze fixed on Sieglinde, who continues silently embarrassed.

lg.l: Hunding here will I wait for.

p.hi: Sieglinde starts, listens and hears Hunding outside leading his horse to the stable. She hurries to the door and opens it. Hunding, armed with shield and spear, enters, but, perceiving Siegmund, pauses on the threshold. Hunding turns with a look of stern inquiry to Sieglinde.

lg.l: I gave him, as a guest,

div.p: [To Sieglinde, as he takes off his armour and hands it to her.
Set the meal for us men!
[Sieglinde hangs up the arms on the stem of the ash-tree, fetches food and drink from the store-room and sets supper on the table. Involuntarily she turns her gaze on Siegmund again.
HUNDING
[Examining Siegmund's features keenly and with amaze, compares them with Sieglinde's. Aside.

lg.l: Gleams the guile of the serpent.

div.p: [He conceals his surprise, and turns with apparent unconcern to Siegmund.

lg.l: I ran by I know not what road.
And I would gladly be told.
HUNDING [At table, inviting Siegmund to be seated.
Who guard the honour of Hunding.
May I ask of my guest
In return to tell me his name?

div.p: [Siegmund, who has taken his seat at the table, looks thoughtfully before him. Sieglinde, who has placed herself beside Hunding and opposite Siegmund, gazes at him with evident sympathy and suspense.
Hunding discovers the likeness between Siegmund and Sieglinde.

lg.l: To this woman tell thy secret:
SIEGMUND [Looks up and, gazing into her eyes, begins gravely.
Not for me the name Friedmund;
But forced was I to be Wehwalt.
And I am one of twins:
With a sister twin I was born.
Her who gave me my life,
Nor her with whom I was born.
Went the son with the father.
And found the wolf's nest robbed.
Had dealt us this bitter blow.
Sore beset and harried were they,
But boldly battled the pair of wolves.

div.p: [Turning to Hunding.

lg.l: A Wölfing tells thee the tale,
And a well-known Wölfing, I trow.
I think that dark rumours anent
This doughty pair have reached me,
Like chaff we scattered the foe.
But trace of my father I lost;
In the woods I could not stay;
My heart longed for men and for women.—
Still I was branded an outlaw;
For woe was all that was mine.

div.p: [He looks at Sieglinde and marks her sympathetic gaze.

lg.l: Thou wert shown no grace by the Norns
No one greets thee as guest
At last thy weapon was lost!
To one whom her heart did not choose.
Fordone and dead lay the brothers.
The slain were embraced by the maid,
She wept wild streams of woe,
And bathed the dead with her tears;
For the loss of her brothers slain
I fled from the furious host—
She lay lifeless on the dead.

div.p: [To Sieglinde with a look of fervent sorrow.

lg.l: The reason now I have told
Why none may know me as Friedmund.

div.p: [He rises and walks to the hearth. Pale and deeply moved, Sieglinde looks on the ground.

lg.l: All hate it, and I with the rest.
When forth in haste I was summoned,
For the night thou art my guest.
I choose the day for the fight:
Thy life shall pay for the dead.

div.p: [To Sieglinde, who steps between the two men with anxious gestures; harshly.

lg.l: Prepare my draught for the night,

div.p: [Sieglinde stands for a while undecided and thoughtful. Slowly and with hesitating steps she goes towards the store-room, There she pauses again, lost in thought, her face half averted. With quiet resolution she opens the cupboard, fills a drinking-horn, and shakes spices into it out of a box. She then turns her eyes on Siegmund, in order to meet his gaze, which he never removes from her. She perceives that Hunding is watching, and proceeds immediately to the bed-chamber. On the steps she turns once more, looks yearningly at Siegmund, and indicates with her eyes, persistently and with speaking plainness, a particular spot in the stem of the ash-tree. Hunding starts, and drives her off with a violent gesture. With a last look at Siegmund, she disappears into the bed-chamber, and shuts the door behind her.

lg.l: HUNDING [Taking his weapons from the tree-stem.
With weapons man should be armed.

div.p: [He goes into bed-chamber. The shooting of the bolt is heard from within.

[Siegmund alone. It has grown quite dark. All the light in the hall comes from a dull fire on the hearth. Siegmund sinks down on to a couch beside the fire and broods forsome time silently in great agitation.

lg.l: My father said when most wanted
A sword I should find and wield.
The woman for whom I long—
She whose charm both wounds and
In thrall is held by the man
When from my bosom should burst
The fury that fills my heart?

div.p: [The fire collapses. From the flame which leaps up a bright light falls on the spot in the ash-tree's stem indicated by Sieglinde's look, and on which the hilt of a sword is now plainly visible.
Sieglinde prepares Hunding's draught for the night
[From this point the fire gradually goes out.

lg.l: Till by the hills it was hid.

div.p: [The fire flickers up faintly again.

lg.l: But once more, ere it set,
Was lit by its golden glow.

div.p: [The fire goes out altogether. Total darkness. The door of the bed-chamber opens noiselessly. Sieglinde comes out in a white garment and advances softly but quickly towards the hearth.

lg.l: The draught that I mixed him I drugged.
Use to good purpose the night!
I have come to show thee a weapon;
O couldst thou make it thine!
O hearken: heed what I tell thee!
One who was bartered by thieves.
That one of his eyes was hidden;
As he swung a sword in his hands.
To the hilt driving it home.
The weapon he gains in guerdon
Who draws it from its place.
Could win the weapon for his;
The strongest tugged at the steel;
Not an inch it stirred in the stem;
I knew then who he was
The sword was stuck in the tree.
Could I but find the dear friend,
And clasp him close in my arms!
Both woman and sword are his.
That welds us twain into one.
That once failed me I find.
Holding thee, love, in my arms thus,
Feeling the beat of thy heart!

div.p: [The outer door swings open.

lg.l: SIEGLINDE [With a start of alarm tears herself away.
Ha, who went? Who entered there?

div.p: [The door remains open. Outside a glorious spring night. The full moon shines in, throwing its bright light on the pair, so that they can suddenly see one another quite plainly.
[He draws Sieglinde with tender force on to the couch, so that she sits beside him. The moon shines more and more brightly.

lg.l: When blithe the birds are singing
From her warm blood blossom flowers
At last the door should have opened,
By love has spring been allured;
Now glad she laughs to the light.
Lo! Love is mated with spring!
That I used to pine for,
When pinched by the winter frost;
When thy first glance fell on me sweetly
All I had seen appeared strange;
I never seemed to have known
And I saw thou wert mine
What I hid in my heart,
My eyes first beheld a friend.

div.p: [She hangs enraptured on his neck, and looks him close in the face.

lg.l: And so sweetly sways every sense!

div.p: [Pushing the hair back from his brow, regards him with astonishment.

lg.l: The man I first saw to-day
Again I see it before me;
As in the pool it arose
But no! I heard the sound lately,
When he greeted me had that eye—
And almost addressed him as father.

div.p: [After a pause.

lg.l: My sway is o'er bliss not sorrow!
Thou wouldst have me be known by:
Thy choice will also be mine!
The name of thy father was Wölfe?
A wolf to the fearful foxes!
Which, fairest one, shines in thine own,
Then let my love call thee
Come forth from thy scabbard to me!

div.p: [He draws the sword with a violent effort from the stem of the tree and shows it to the amazed and enraptured Sieglinde.

lg.l: From the house of his foe.
Thy shield be Nothung, the sword,
When Siegmund is captive to love!

div.p: [He throws his arm round her so as to draw her forth with him.

lg.l: As well as the sword thou hast

div.p: [She throws herself on his breast.

lg.l: So Wälsungs shall flourish for aye!

div.p: [He draws her to him with fervent passion. The curtain falls quickly.

div.head: THE SECOND ACT

p.hi: A wild, mountainous spot. In the background a gorge rises from below to a high ridge of rocks, from which the ground slopes down again towards the front. Wotan, in full armour, carrying his spear. Before him Brünnhilde as a Valkyrie, also fully armed.

lg.l: And cause the Wälsung to win!
No place in Walhall has he.
BRÜNNHILDE [Ascends the height on the right, shouting

l.hi: and springing from rock to rock.

div.p: [She pauses on a high peak, looks down into the gorge and calls back to Wotan.

lg.l: Drawn hither in her car by her rams,
Hot she hastes to the fray.
The battle alone thou must brave;
I go; thou art left in the lurch!

div.p: [She disappears behind the mountain peak at the side. Fricka, in a car drawn by a pair of rams, has driven up the gorge to the mountain ridge, where she suddenly stops, alights and strides angrily towards Wotan in the foreground.

lg.l: WOTAN [Aside, when he sees Fricka approaching.
But I must act with firmness
FRICKA [Moderating her pace as she approaches, and
I seek thee, where thou dost hide
That help in need thou may'st promise.
Who boldly wrought him the wrong.
None pays for love's might to me.
How dull and how deaf thou wouldst seem!
As though thou wert not aware
Profaned so rudely I grieve for.
For where bold natures are stirring
I urge them frankly to strife.

div.p: Brünnhilde

lg.l: From bond of a twin-born pair!
Of brother and sister as lovers?
So take advice and be wise!
If thou wilt, laughing on love,
FRICKA [With a burst of deep indignation.
The fruit of thy lawless love,
May in wantonness flourish and rule!
Since by thee the first they are scorned!
As thy fickle fancy allures thee,
While grief is gnawing my heart.
For, thy wife still holding in awe,
Thou didst give her as maids
Even Brünnhilde, bride of thy Wish.
Now thy wife at the feet
Of whelps of a wolf thou dost fling!
Mock and trample now the betrayed one!

div.p: Fricka approaches in anger.

lg.l: To thee there is nothing plain
Till day has dawned on the deed,
On things not yet brought forth.
A hero gods have not shielded,
And who is not bound by their law.
Were he fit for the deed
Yet which must be done for the gods.
That was beyond the strength of the gods,
By whose grace alone he is strong?
Who breathed their souls into men?
Who opened their eyes, that they see?
And is bold through thee alone.
That thou gavest to thy son.

div.p: [From here Wotan's whole attitude expresses an ever-deepening uneasiness and gloom.

lg.l: And the need came from thee.
Which led him where it lay hid?

div.p: [Wotan makes a wrathful gesture. Fricka goes on more and more confidently as she sees the impression produced on him.

lg.l: But Siegmund is mine as my slave.

div.p: [Another violent gesture from Wotan, who then seems to succumb to the feeling of his own powerlessness.

lg.l: A goddess, to suffer such shame!
Thou wilt grant him no aid,
When to arms the avenger calls?
The Valkyrie turn from him too.
BRÜNNHILDE [Is heard calling from the heights.
For Siegmund I called her to horse.

div.p: [Brünnhilde appears with her horse on the rocky path to the right. When she sees Fricka she stops abruptly and, during the following, slowly and silently leads her horse down the path. She then puts it in a cave.

lg.l: Perish and pass would the Gods
The Wälsung falls for my honour.
Does Wotan now pledge me his oath?
WOTAN [Throwing himself on to a rocky seat in terrible dejection.

div.p: [Fricka strides towards the back, where she meets Brünnhilde and halts for a moment before her.
[She drives off quickly.
BRÜNNHILDE
[Comes forward anxious and wondering to Wotan, who leaning back on his rocky seat, is brooding gloomily.

lg.l: WOTAN [Dropping his arm helplessly and sinking his head on his breast.
I, least free of all living!

div.p: [His expression and gestures working up, from this point, to a fearful outburst.

lg.l: Most sorrowful I of all living!

div.p: [Alarmed, throws her shield, spear and helmet from her and kneels with anxious affection at his feet.

lg.l: With dismay thou art filling thy child!

div.p: [She lays her head and hands with tender anxiety on his knees and breast.
WOTAN
[Looks long in her eyes, then strokes her hair with involuntary tenderness. As if coming out of a deep reverie, he at last begins, very softly.

lg.l: The controlling might of my will?
If I am not thy will?

div.p: Brünnhilde slowly and silently leads her horse down the path to the cave

lg.l: What never to any was spoken
Shall be unspoken now and for ever.

div.p: [In a low, muffled voice.

lg.l: When grown mighty still I desired it.
The gleaming gold of the Rhine,
The home the giants had built me,
From which I commanded the world.
Of this doom I was fain
But silent she vanished from sight.
Then my gladness of heart was gone,
The god's one desire was to know.
To the womb of the earth
And compelled her tongue to speak.
Tidings by her I was told;
And with her I left a fair pledge:
Heroes I got ye to gather.
And well filled surely thy halls were;
Many a one I have brought.
With dismay thou art filling thy child!"
I defy the hosts of the night.
Could the runes of the ring
To wrest the ring from the foeman.

div.p: [In a low voice.

lg.l: For which his own brother he slew.
The ring I must needs recover
With which his work I rewarded.
I, who by treaties am lord,
To my treaties also am slave.
Though it was all my desire.
One to fight me, the god,
The other whom I so long for,
The free by themselves must be fashioned,
All that I fashion are slaves!

div.p: [Slowly and bitterly.

lg.l: Now, when the gods seek vengeance,
Shield he has none but the sword
By the grace of a god.
I must bend my will to her wishes.
Loth to let the gold go.
I must always lose what I love most,
Slay what my heart holds dearest,

div.p: [His gestures, at first those of terrible grief end by expressing despair.

lg.l: I wait but one thing more:

div.p: [He pauses thoughtfully.

lg.l: In the strange, wild words of the Wala:
Gets a son in his wrath,
That the dwarf had won a woman,

div.p: [Rising in bitter wrath.

lg.l: What I loathe with deep loathing:
The hollow pomp of the gods.
For what does my own will profit,
Since it cannot fashion a free one?
Wouldst have me shelter the Wälsung.
And fight so that Hunding prevails.
To thy heart was so precious—
I will shield him in spite of
Who art thou—who but the choiceless,
That the creature made by me
Dost thou, child, know my wrath?
That once wore nothing but smiles.
Woe to him whom it strikes!
Dear the price he would pay!

div.p: [He storms away and disappears among the rocks to the left.
Brünnhilde stands for a long time dazed and alarmed

lg.l: BRÜNNHILDE [Stands for a long time dazed and alarmed.
Enraged, but never once like this!

div.p: [She stoops down sadly, takes up her armour and puts it on again.
[She gazes thoughtfully before her.

lg.l: Must the faithful one falsely forsake thee!

div.p: [She turns slowly towards the back.

[On reaching the rocky pass, Brünnhilde, looking down into the gorge, perceives Siegmund and Sieglinde. She watches them for a moment, then turns into the cave where her horse is, so that she is completely hidden from the audience. Siegmund and Sieglinde appear on the pass, Sieglinde hurrying in front. Siegmund tries to stop her.

lg.l: SIEGMUND [Embraces her with tender force, straining
So fleet that I lagged behind:
Thy foot stopped for no call.

div.p: [Sieglinde stares wildly before her.
[Gazes into his eyes with growing rapture, throws her arms passionately round his neck and remains so for some time. She then starts up in wild terror.

lg.l: The foul one who loved one so fair!
And all the love of the man
Was hers who loved him alone—
The thought she once had obeyed.
Scorn to bring on the brother,
All thy wrongs will be avenged!
Of the vows and the wedlock profaned!

div.p: [Gazes before her as if gone crazed.
[She throws herself sobbing on his breast, and presently starts up in terror again.

lg.l: Ha, there! I see thee now!
By the feet they seize thee

div.p: [She falls fainting into his arms.
Brünnhilde with her horse, at the mouth of the cave

[He listens to her breathing, and, when convinced that she still lives, lets her slide down so that, as he himself sinks into a sitting posture, her head rests upon his knees. In this position both remain till the end of the following scene. A long silence, during which Siegmund bends over Sieglinde with tender concern, and presses a long kiss on her brow.

[Brünnhilde, leading her horse, comes out of the cave and walks slowly and solemnly towards the front. She pauses and watches Siegmund from a distance, then advances slowly again and stops when she gets nearer. In one hand she carries her shield and spear, the other rest on her horse's neck, and thus she gravely stands looking at Siegmund.

lg.l: That dost stand so fair and so stern?
Bids farewell to the light of life.

div.p: [Looks into her eyes with a long steadfast and searching gaze, then bows his head in thought and finally turns resolutely to her again.

lg.l: Wine will bring for thy cup.
But one thing tell me, divine one!
Siegmund will find no Sieglinde there!

div.p: [Bends tenderly over Sieglinde, kisses her softly on the brow, and turns again quietly to Brünnhilde.

lg.l: And tell them I will not come!
Thou canst not force me to go!
Fool, what will force thee is death
Fix on him for thy prey.
I think it is he who will fall!
With this sword I laugh at thy threats.
For the magic spell he withdraws!

div.p: [In an outburst of grief he bends tenderly over Sieglinde.

lg.l: Most sad and ill-starred of all true ones!
And I who was all thy defence,
For whom thou the world hast defied—
In battle, thy trust must betray!
And triumph now turns to scorn!

div.p: [He bends low over Sieglinde.
[Slowly and with hesitation.

lg.l: In my heart I know thee
Then gloat and feast thyself full!
Siegmund, thy wife be my charge,
While my wife is living shall guard her.
I will slay the slumberer first!
That she carries of thee and thy love!
That a true man received from a false—
That fails me when facing the foe;
Worthless when turned on the foe,
Will serve me when turned on the friend.

div.p: [He points the sword at Sieglinde.

lg.l: Take them with one fell stroke!
BRÜNNHILDE [With a passionate outburst of sympathy.
And Siegmund too shall be spared!

div.p: [Horns are heard in the distance.

lg.l: On the field again I shall find thee.

div.p: [She rushes away and disappears with her horse down a gorge on the right. Siegmund gazes after her joyful and exultant. The stage has gradually grown dark. Heavy storm-clouds have gathered in the background, and hide the cliffs, gorge, and rocky pass completely from view.

lg.l: SIEGMUND [Bending over Sieglinde, listens to her breathing.
The dear one's pain and grief.
She brought her this blissful repose;
Else would the grimly fought fight
Have terrified one in such woe.
And peace shall end thy pain!

div.p: [He lays her gently on the rocky seat and kisses her brow in farewell. Then, hearing Hunding's horn sound, he starts up with resolution.
[He draws his sword.
Nothung pays him his debt.
[He hastens to the back and, on reaching the pass, immediately disappears in a dark thunder-cloud, from which, the next instant, a flash of lightning breaks.

lg.l: SIEGLINDE [Begins to move uneasily in her dreams.
Would but my father come back!
With the boy he still roams in the wood.

div.p: [She starts up. Violent thunder and lightning.
Siegmund! Ha!
[She stares about her in growing terror. Almost the whole of the stage is veiled by black thunder-clouds. Hunding's horn is heard close at hand.

lg.l: HUNDING'S VOICE [From the mountain pass in the background.
Or with the hounds I will hold thee!
SIEGMUND'S VOICE [From farther back in the gorge.
That I have missed thee thus?
Halt, that I may find thee!
Lest Fricka fail thee at need!
Come and try the taste of its steel!
Hold your hands, ye men there!

div.p: [She rushes towards the pass, but is suddenly dazzled by a light which flashes forth from above the combatants to the right, and staggers aside as if blinded.

[Brünnhilde appears in the glare of light, floating above Siegmund, and protecting him with her shield. Just as Siegmund is aiming a deadly blow at Hunding a glowing red light breaks through the clouds from the left, in which Wotan appears, standing over Hunding and holding his spear across in front of Siegmund.

[Brünnhilde with her shield recoils in terror before Wotan; Siegmund's sword breaks in splinters on the outstretched spear. Hunding plunges his sword into the disarmed man's breast. Siegmund falls down dead, and Sieglinde, who has heard his death-sigh, sinks to the ground as if lifeless. With Siegmund's fall the lights on both sides disappear. Dense clouds shroud all but the foreground in darkness. Through these Brünnhilde is dimly seen turning in wild haste to Sieglinde.

lg.l: To horse, that I may save thee!

div.p: [She lifts Sieglinde up quickly on to her horse, which is standing near the side ravine, and immediately disappears. Thereupon the clouds divide in the middle, so that Hunding, who has just drawn his sword out of Siegmund's breast, is distinctly seen. Wotan, surrounded by clouds, stands on a rock behind, leaning on his spear and gazing sorrowfully on Siegmund's body.

lg.l: Has slain what mocked her might.

div.p: [Before the contemptuous wave of his hand Hunding falls dead to the ground. Suddenly breaking out in terrible anger.
[He vanishes with thunder and lightning. The curtain falls quickly.

div.head: On the top of a rocky mountain

p.hi: On the right the stage is bounded by a pine-wood. On the left is the entrance to a cave, above which the rock rises to its highest point. At the back the view is quite open. Rocks of varying heights form the edge of the precipice. Clouds fly at intervals past the mountain peak as if driven by storm. Gerhilde, Ortlinde, Waltraute, and Schwertleite have taken up their position on the rocky peak above the cave. They are in full armour.

div.p: GERHILDE
[On the highest point, calling towards the background, where a dense cloud is passing.
[A flash of lightning comes from the cloud, showing a Valkyrie on horseback, on whose saddle hangs a slain warrior. The apparition, approaching the cliff, passes from left to right.

lg.l: GERHILDE, WALTRAUTE AND SCHWERTLEITE [Calling to her as she draws near.

div.p: [The cloud with the apparition vanishes to the right behind the wood.

lg.l: GERHILDE [Descending a little towards the others.
ORTLINDE [Springs up and runs to the wood.
The horse is kicking my mare!
GERHILDE [Laughing aloud with HELMWIGE AND SCHWERTLEITE.

div.p: [On the highest point, where listening towards the right she has taken Gerhilde's place as watcher, calling towards the right-hand side of the background.

lg.l: SIEGRUNE'S VOICE [From the back on the right.

div.p: [In answer, their gestures, as well as a bright light behind the wood, showing that Siegrune has just arrived there.

lg.l: GRIMGERDE'S AND ROSSWEISSE'S VOICES [From the back on the left.

div.p: [In a cloud which passes across the stage from the left, and from which lightning flashes, Rossweisse and Grimgerde appear, also on horseback, each carrying a slain warrior on her saddle.
HELMWIGE, GERLINDE AND SIEGRUNE
[Have come out of the wood and wave their hands from the edge of the precipice to Rossweisse and Grimgerde, who disappear behind the wood.

lg.l: ROSSWEISSE AND GRIMGERDE [Coming out of the wood.
Went ye twain on one quest?
SIEGRUNE [On the look-out, calling towards the back.

div.p: [To the others.

lg.l: THE VALKYRIES [All hasten to the look-out.*

div.p: [They watch her with growing astonishment.
[Helmwige and Gerhilde run to the wood, followed by Siegrune and Rossweisse.

lg.l: THE OTHER VALKYRIES [Running into the wood.

div.p: [The Valkyries all return to the stage; Brünnhilde accompanies them, leading and supporting Sieglinde.

lg.l: Thus ride they only who flee.
I flee for the first time
BRÜNNHILDE [Turns and looks out anxiously, then comes back.

div.p: [Ortlinde and Waltraute spring up the peak to the look-out.

lg.l: He nears, he nears, in fury!
He nears, he nears, in fury!
Who slew him himself with his spear.
I hastened, O my sisters, to you!
From the north like the night.
That forth the woman may fly?

div.p: [Who until now has been staring gloomily and coldly before her, starts up with a repellent gesture as Brünnhilde encircles her with a warm, protective embrace.

lg.l: Death is all that I crave.
Who bade thee thus bear me?
Thou must hearken, maid, to my prayer:
Pierce thou my heart with thy sword!
The Wälsung's child thou shalt bear!

div.p: [Gives a violent start; suddenly her face beams with sublime joy.
[An ever-darkening thunderstorm nears from the back.

lg.l: Till I know thee past reach of his rage.
Say, whither shall my flight be?
And keeps far from the place.
Hideth, O woman, thy sheltering womb!

div.p: [She takes the pieces of Siegmund's sword from under her breast-plate and gives them to Sieglinde.

lg.l: From the field where slain was
Be blest by Sieglind' in woe!

div.p: [She hastens away to the right in front. The rocky peak is surrounded by black thunder-clouds. A fearful storm rages from the back. A fiery glow increases in strength to the right.

lg.l: ORTLINDE AND WALTRAUTE [Coming down from the look-out.

div.p: [Brünnhilde, after following Sieglinde with her eyes for a while, goes towards the background, looks into the wood, and comes forward again fearfully.

lg.l: Unless ye ward off its weight.

div.p: [Fly towards the rocky point in fear, drawing Brünnhilde with them.
[They hide Brünnhilde in their midst and look anxiously towards the wood, which is now lit up by a bright fiery glow, while in the background it has grown quite dark.
[Comes from the wood in a terrible state of wrath and excitement and goes towards the Valkyries on the height, looking angrily for Brünnhilde.

lg.l: Fearful and loud thy rage is!
By what misdeed have thy daughters
To us fled the pursued one,
In her need praying for help,
That thy first wild rage be calmed.
For this have I reared you
That ye wild ones might weep and whine
When my wrath on a faithless one falls?
Knew what most deeply I brooded;
Pierced to the source of my being;
All, I wished to be, came to birth.
And against me pointed the spear
That she held from me alone.
Life and name as my gift!
Dost hide from me in terror,
A coward who shirks her doom?

div.p: [Steps out from the band of Valkyries, and humbly but with a firm step descends from the rocky peak until within a short distance from Wotan.

lg.l: Thou hast shaped thy doom for thyself.
Yet against my will thou hast worked;
Yet against me thou hast commanded;
Yet thy wish has dared to cross mine;
Yet against me raised was thy shield;
Against me the lot thou hast chosen;
Thou hast roused up heroes against me.
No more shall I send thee from Walhall
When the high Gods sit at banquet,
Our bond is broken in twain,
And from my sight henceforth thou now

div.p: [Leave their places in the excitement, and come a little farther down the rocks.

lg.l: Conquering thee, one shall take all!
The man who chances this way
And awakes her, shall master the maid.

div.p: [Come down from the height in great excitement, and in terrified groups surround Brünnhilde, who lies half kneeling before Wotan.

lg.l: For as sisters share we her shame.
Shall your traitorous sister be banished,
Through the clouds her swift steed to the
Beside the hearth she will spin,
To all mockers a mark for scorn.

div.p: The ride of the Valkyries
[Brünnhilde sinks with a cry to the ground. The Valkyries, horror-stricken, recoil from her violently.

lg.l: Then fly from the lost one!
The fool shall share the same doom:
I warn you, ye bold ones, well!
Get ye gone at a gallop,
Trouble is rife else for you here!
THE VALKYRIES [Separate with a wild cry and rush into the wood.

div.p: [Black clouds settle thickly on the cliff; a rushing sound is heard in the wood. From the clouds breaks a vivid flash of lightning, by which the Valkyries are seen packed closely together, and riding wildly away with loose bridles. The storm soon subsides; the thunder-clouds gradually disperse. In the following scene the weather becomes fine again and twilight falls, followed at the close by night.
[Wotan and Brünnhilde, who lies stretched at his feet, remain behind alone. A long solemn silence.
BRÜNNHILDE
[Begins to raise her head a little, and, commencing timidly, gains confidence as she proceeds.

lg.l: That to such shame the offender should be
That I must suffer abasement so low?
That it must rob me of honour for aye?

div.p: [She raises herself gradually to a kneeling posture.

lg.l: It costs thee thy favourite child!
WOTAN [His attitude unchanged, gravely and gloomily.
And that will show thee thy guilt!
Didst thou fight for the Wälsung?
Thou wert a foe to thyself.
I thought thou didst understand me,
If I had not treason to punish
Thou wouldst be unworthy my wrath.
But I knew well this one thing—
That thy love was the Wälsung's;
This one thing thou hadst forgotten.
That Siegmund might not be shielded.
Blindly thy back on him turning!
From the foe in the field,
That which stirred the heart in my breast
Was how I could serve him;
Who taught my heart this love,
By the Wälsung's side as friend—
What I yearned so greatly to do—
In my tortured heart I imprisoned?
When I turned, to my torment,
The fearful design in me woke
In the ruins of my own world

div.p: [Somewhat freely.

lg.l: While I drank of divine woe

div.p: [Dryly and shortly.

lg.l: From me thou hast turned away!
And so long as life lasts
I, the God, dare nevermore greet thee!
To love what was loved by thee.
Where I shall not find thee,
A half once thine and thine only,
Were I a target for scorn!
If I must go from Walhall,
No more in thy work be a sharer,
With Wotan no part hast thou—
By thee has been founded a race
Too glorious to bring forth a coward
One day must a matchless hero
Name not the Wälsungs to me!
Through envy they came to naught.

div.p: [With an air of secrecy.

lg.l: Nor for fruit that she may bear.
And that I splintered with my spear.
I cannot choose it or change!
Too long I stay by thy side.
Wife thou shalt be to the man
Who finds and wakes thee from sleep!
This one thing that in deep anguish
I plead for thou must accord!

div.p: [Firmly.

lg.l: Encircle the rock with thy flame!
But, cruel one, expose her not

div.p: [With wild ecstasy.
[Overcome and deeply stirred, turns quickly towards Brünnhilde, raises her from her knees and looks into her eyes with emotion.
[Passionately.

lg.l: Nor bring me mead at banquet?
The laughing delight of my eyes,
Than ever yet burned for a bride!
One only shall set the bride free,
One freer than I, the God!

div.p: [Moved and enraptured, Brünnhilde sinks on the breast of Wotan, who holds her in a long embrace; then she throws back her head again, and, still embracing him, gazes into his eyes with emotion and awe.

lg.l: Those eyes so lovely and bright
That oft with smiles I caressed,
The praise of heroes I heard:
Those eyes so radiant and fair
That oft in storm on me shone,
Of the world I longed for,
While fears thronged thick around me—
Must they close, and for ever!

div.p: [He takes her head in both hands.
As he moves slowly away, Wotan turns and looks sorrowfully back at Brünnhilde.

[He kisses her long on the eyes, and with these closed she sinks back softly into his arms, unconscious. He carries her gently to a low mossy mound, and lays her there beneath the broad-spreading pine-tree which overshadows it. He gazes at her and closes her helmet; his eyes then rest on the form of the sleeper, which he completely covers with the great steel shield of the Valkyries. Having done so, he moves slowly away, turning to take one more sorrowful look. Then he strides with solemn resolve to the middle of the stage, and points his sword towards a large rock.

lg.l: I who found thee at first
And from whom thou didst vanish
Encircle the rock with thy flame!

div.p: [He strikes the rock three times with his spear during the following.
Loge! Loge! Appear!

[A gleam of fire issues from the stone and gradually becomes a fiery glow; then flickering flames break forth. Soon wild, shooting flames surround Wotan, who, with his spear, directs the sea of fire to encircle the rock. It spreads towards the background, so that the mountain is surrounded by flame.
[He stretches out his spear as a ban, looks sorrowfully back at Brünnhilde, then moves slowly away, turning his head for a farewell gaze. Finally he disappears through the fire. The curtain falls.
The sleep of Brünnhilde
